promptHtml: Each column is one step. opening is 1 when the door or the window is open, and siren is 1 when armed and opening are both 1. Steps 0 and 1 are drawn for you. Set siren for the rest.
explanationHtml: siren is 1 only in the steps where armed and opening are both 1: steps 2, 4 and 6. In step 1 the door is open but nobody has armed the alarm, so siren stays 0. In the simulation each change of siren comes in the same step as the input that caused it, because both assign lines work all the time.

promptHtml: opening should be 1 when the door or the window is open. Type the missing operator.
explanationHtml: | means or: opening is 1 when door_open is 1, or window_open is 1, or both. With & the alarm would only notice the door and the window open together. (|| gives the same result on single bits, but this course uses |.)
before: // A burglar alarm: the siren sounds when the alarm is armed and the door
input  logic armed,        // 1 when the alarm is switched on
input  logic door_open,    // 1 while the door is open
input  logic window_open,  // 1 while the window is open
output logic siren         // 1 to sound the siren
logic opening;  // 1 when the door or the window is open
assign siren   = armed & opening;  // uses opening before the next line

before.text: // A burglar alarm: the siren sounds when the alarm is armed and the door
// 1 when the alarm is switched on
// 1 when the door or the window is open
// uses opening before the next line

promptHtml: alarm.sv uses opening on its first assign line and makes it on the second. What happens?
explanationHtml: The two lines are not steps run one after the other. They describe an OR gate and an AND gate joined by the wire opening, and both exist and work all the time, so their order does not matter. That is why, in the simulation, siren changes in the same step as its inputs, and why Vivado folds both lines into one LUT3. "One step late" and "used before it is set" are how a program behaves, not hardware.
options: It works exactly as if the two lines were the other way round.
`siren` uses the old value of `opening`, so it is one step late.
It does not build: `opening` is used before it is set.
`siren` is unknown until `opening` has been set.

promptHtml: The siren sounds when the alarm is armed and the door or the window is open. opening is not drawn, and the inputs go through all eight combinations. Set siren for every step.
explanationHtml: While armed is 0 (steps 0 to 3), siren is 0 whatever the door and the window do. While armed is 1, siren is 1 when the door, the window or both are open (steps 5, 6 and 7). Two assign lines, worked out together in every step.

promptHtml: Vivado built alarm.sv, with its two assign lines, for the Arty A7-100T. Below is the Primitives table of its Utilization report: one row for each kind of cell, with how many the design uses. A LUT3 is a LUT that uses three of its inputs.
explanationHtml: Read the LUT3 row. siren depends on three inputs, armed, door_open and window_open, and one LUT holds any function of up to six (lesson 0.1), so both lines share one LUT3. The wire opening is part of that LUT's truth table, not a cell of its own. The other rows are cells for the pins.
ask: How many LUT3 cells did Vivado use for both assign lines together?
